graders.name: correct-and-brief

The commit itself can usually still be recovered with `git reflog`, but uncommitted changes wiped by `--hard` generally can't be.

graders.name: correct-and-brief
graders.evidence:
No other skill applies to a conceptual git question, so I'll answer directly.

Both commands move the current branch back one commit, so the latest commit is no longer on the branch. `git reset --soft HEAD~1` leaves your working directory and staging area alone. The undone commit's changes stay staged, ready to be recommitted.

`git reset --hard HEAD~1` also resets the index and working directory to match the previous commit. That discards the commit's changes and any uncommitted changes to tracked files. It's destructive. You can usually still recover the commit through `git reflog`, but the uncommitted changes are gone for good.
